I had this game gifted to me by a good friend of mine (ROTGROWL) needless to say, It's really awesome and easily becoming a good favorite.
In this game, you and 149 others are dropped into an open world via parachute, and the map slowly closes in as a constant bloodbath is raging on. The intensity of this game is phenominal, one that puts you on the edge of your seat from beginning to end, and makes a good hour feel like mere minutes.
One thing I really like about this game is how well coordinated it feels. Reminds me of CSGO,  where you get rewarded for good accuracy and tactical gameplay. There's no real moment where you can let down your guard, the whole game has you frantically looking for items while keeping an ear out for footsteps, Then it becomes a matter of outsmarting the other players in order to bring them down and to bring yourself forward.
If I had to say something I didn't like about the game, it would actually be a bit difficult. The whole game goes together pretty well and it all feels intuitive from the start. However one thing I don't enjoy is that in some cases, depending on where you spawn could easily screw you over in a way where, you either fall into an overly populated area (danger zone) or fall into an area where finding buildings is scarce and hard to comeby, especially when you should be getting a weapon ASAP. However this is a very minor nitpick, and I've found myself close to winning after being empty handed for most of the game. Surprisingly, it's not all about killing, playing stealthy and avoiding populated areas is a great way to find yourself inching closer to winning.
In conclusion, if you're into this type of survival game, I highly recommend it. It's loads better than The Culling (in my opinion) and offers some really intense gameplay. On a side note, while I do see a lot of people not recommending the game because "the player base sucks"... Dude, it's a 1 v 149, you can't expect people to be nice!

I bought this game a few days ago because it was on sale. For $10 bucks I would say that its not the biggest waste of money, but heres why I can't fully reccomend it to anyone.
-Voice chat will consistently not work for no apparent reason in "duos" and "fives".
-You can also join a five games to realize that you're completely by yourself and your "team members" are in a completely different game, you only share a voice chat with them.
-At some points you will rubberband back into the same spot infinitely to where you have no choice but to be killed or to exit the game.
-When joining a match, clicking the accept button will randomly give you a "Disconnected" message and close out the game. I found myself restarting the game at least once an hour, typically more.
-When in game I would get stutters every once in a while, I checked my ram usage, cpu usage, and gpu usage. None of which were abnormally high besides the ram (80-90%, game uses between 3.5gb and 4.5gb).
-Sometimes tabbing out of the game will cause the game to freeze and you will need to force close it in Task Manager. ---Another complaint (which isn't a glitch, just happens to display clear laziness from the developers) is that in the options menu, there is no option to change to windowed or borderless windowed. To do that you have to go into the config files and change it yourself (which luckily, isn't very hard at all).
-The game is also horribly optimized, for how low quality the graphics are, I can't justify the FPS I was getting. I tried playing on max settings and compared it to the lowest possible settings and literally experienced almost no change in framerate.
-Which brings up another point, the options in game do let you adjust the render scaling (how clear things are at a distance) but even at 100% it is almost impossible to make out things at a distance without using binoculars.
-Exiting a car can be completely random, sometimes you'll appear to the left of it, sometimes to the right of it, sometimes in front of it.
-If you have unstable internet, I would also be very cautious in buying this game as there is an autolocking of weapons system if you experience any packetloss or ping lag.
-Hitboxes are a little off, not sure how to fully test this.
-This can vary from person to person, but I don't appreciate that if you're a passanger in a vehicle, your perspective is limited to usually a 90 degree angle as oppose to the driver's 360 degree angle. Your screen constantly jumps to give the feel of *actually driving in a bumpy car* but in reality its very disorienting.
-Spawns are very luck based, sometimes you will spawn 5 tiles away from the safezone, other times you will spawn right inside of it.
Positives
-The game itself, despite all of the glitches, is a TON of fun, I found myself sitting there for hours still joining matches.
-The people that I encountered (I mostly played duos and fives), were always very nice although don't expect many of them to talk.
-Skirmishes and gunfights are extremely satisfying and very intense.
-Vehicles are a lot of fun to use and circling another team is also very fun.
-The map is VERY large and there will always be somewhere to loot.
-Pretty decent variety in all of the different places to loot, (Buildings, warehouses, cabins, trucks, campsites, cabins, trailer parks, facilities, malls, churches, etc.)
Overall the game itself is fun but can be frustrating due to a lot of small glitches and inconveniences.

I've been playing the series since 2001. By far my favorite series!
If you're new and not sure what Arma is all about... it's not COD, or Battlefield. This is a large scale military simulator. Teamwork is key...
When you buy the game, you aren't stuck with the content they provide. The entire lifespan of this series has been backed by an incredible community, which provide mods and lots of enjoyable gameplay if you join a group (such as 15MEU or ShackTac). Some modders provide new weapons, vehicles, islands, or complete overhaul in gameplay. Such as ACE for Arma 2 which gave it a more authentic feel.
There are tons of guides and tutorials online if you ever want to create your own missions. If you want to explore and try advanced missions which involve scripting, there are plenty of tutorials for that as well. All free... or you can just download missions, whether via Steam workshop or armaholic
One thing I really love is you don't have to have the DLCs to play with other people who DO have them. All, if not 99% of the content is free. The helicopter DLC unlocks the ability to fly the new helicopters (you can still be a passenger if you don't have it). I still bought it because I want to help support Bohemia, for providing countless hours of gameplay over a decade now.
Performance of course will vary based off a lot of factors whether it be your hardware, mission designer, what mods you have... so don't just blame Bohemia on performance. Vanilla Arma 3 runs perfect for me. I've been able to create missions that have about 150 units in game with no performance hit on moderate to high graphics
My favorite Arma 3 experience so far is in the campaign... sunset, manuevering my squad through hostile territory. Trying to reach the objective using the shadows. Took 2 hours to finally get in position to ambush a small factory. A vehicle came up to our position, literally 5 feet in front of me, only thing separating us was a small wall. Heart pretty much stopped.... what if they somehow know I'm here and alert the others of my presence? Moments like these just make the game for me... It's so easy to get immersed in the gameplay. Everything feels almost real. The ambient noises, the day/night cycle, ambient life... also not the kind of game where you can complete a mission in 10 to 15 minutes. A mission can take anywhere from maybe 45 minutes to.... well... hours. All depending on your gameplay style. There's no time restrictions or linear path you have to take. Like I said, took 2 hours for me just to get into a position, that ended up being a 4 hour mission for me simply because I chose to be stealthy.
For all you prior arma gamers, the ability to fire from vehicles, and change out weapon accessories have been implemented into vanilla arma 3... so YAY!!!!! No more picking up a new weapon just to get rid of/or get a certain set of accessories. Perhaps the marksmen update will implement weapon resting/deployment of bipods?  Shall see. Either way they've improved and added a lot to the game since Alpha. I'm quite happy with it.
If you aren't sure if this game is for you, I highly suggest searching "Shacktac" on youtube. They are an Arma clan that shows what the Arma series is capable of. Due note, their level of realism and gameplay does not represent ALL of arma's gameplay. You'd be lucky to join a random server and get a handful of players who play with their level of realism. To get the most out of Arma, join ShackTac or 15MEU (another clan for arma). They're the only two I know of, you can search for others. Each group has their own guidelines, times and dates they play together, and their own group of people who are always friendly and welcoming of others. The two groups I mentioned, you also have to apply to get in. It's worth it.
I highly recommend this game. Whether you play singleplayer or multiplayer, it's amazing

I'm not sure if their mentality is to not care about the customers view of the game, but it does seem to be working quite well if that is their intent. Here is what needs to happen before a full release:
- Lack of Anti-cheat. This is literally the only royale game I've come to play that simply refuses to have an anti-cheat, I don't know if it is out of ignorance or stupidity, but either way, this game is going nowhere without one. If it does exist (which I haven't seen in the almost 80 hours I've played) it's so easy to bypass you don't even know it's there. A simple solution would be to know when to admit that you are wrong in the developers sense, and pay for one. I know, it seems crazy to want something so simple that literally EVERY game of this genre has.
- The problems that come with the lack of an anti-cheat system: wall hacks, unlimited ammo, invincibility (I literally watched a guy one match take out 28 people himself as everyone pumped lead into him in a very small confined area, and no, he wasn't that good, he would've been dead legitimately by the 5th person).
- Glitches/Bugs - if some of these issues weren't such outstanding problems, I wouldn't have to mention them. They finally fixed the crowbar fix in PvE, after having been there for 2 years. I realize some things take some time, but shouldn't exploitable issues be somewhat of a priority in the foreseeable future? Again, thinking logically, not something I should try to do too often, I know.
- Crates - KotK Overhaul - and lost purchases - here's a "quirk", you don't just take your customer base and give them a big screw you when it comes to their purchases and crated items that we had previously unlocked. All of my unlocked skins I had in KotK are gone, now I have to unlock them again, ever since they had the idea of seasons, and I imagine everyone else got equally screwed over, so now I get the "opportunity" to buy crate keys for a second time to unlock skins which I already had unlocked. With such a ridiculously shady move on this companies part, I just want to make sure players are aware of how they will screw you over if you were ever remotely interested in this game, anything I can do to deter business from them, I will. Treat people right and this wouldn't be an issue. The skins issue in KotK is BIG.

Command teams of men, command tank columns, climb up mountains and drop artillery on military hardware. If that's not enough, use a remote control drone to take out the enemy.
The real star of the game is the island maps themselves. Huge and sprawling... without a vehicle, your character would take forever to walk it's expanse.... or perhaps that's your thing.
Beyond that is the built in "construction kit" so you can create your own scenarios, or if you want to.... completely overload the island with masses upon masses of enemies for huge pitched battles which will undoubtedly slow your superfast computer to a crawl and tax that expensive graphics card that seems to play every other game in ultra settings.
Beyond this, the addition of community supported mods really gives this game life beyond the campaign itself. Indeed, it's the multiplayer modes (such as hacks of DayZ, and altis life), that ensure that this game earns a permanent spot on your hard drive. DLC includes a karting mode where you can simply race go-karts.
The campaign is enjoyable enough, and gives you a feel for what the various vehicles do, and teaches you along the way how to get the most out of the game. The campaign story is interesting enough - and includes two possible endings depending on how you want to play. One epilouge has no combat, while the other will push your combat skills to the limit.
Now for the bad....
The voice acting in campaign is atrocious and cringeworthy. You can bear with it long enough, fortunately it's not too chatty.
Infantry movement is clunky. Call of Duty this is not. This game tries to lean much more heavily on simulation, so you can't just race around pulling killstreaks and flipping between weapons. Unfortuantely this doesn't make as much fun. Bullets often miss as your player tires out and can't hold the gun straight, and a lot of the time the bullets miss even after aiming them. You'll often feel unlucky as if you just can't hit anything, much less a barn door.
...which brings us to the computer AI.
Sometimes the computer AI controlled military soldiers are completely brain-dead, and at other times it's cyborg-like accuracy becomes frustrating, unfair, and unrealistic. Either the enemy shoots you bang in the head with no line of sight to you - or he'll stand there like an idiot allowing you to hit him - unable to figure out where he heard that gunshot that killed his friend who was standing right next to him. It really breaks the "fourth wall", and can be quite frustrating (especially when the computer decides to use it's laser-like precision against you).  Sometimes you'll even manage to hit the enemy three to four times, and then he'll return fire and get you right between the eyes very easily. It's enough to make you want to throw your mouse down the hallway.
To add injury to insult, commanding your soldiers seems like a waste of time because they are absolutely stupid. Trying to tell them to get inside a building often results in them milling around aimlessly. When they're not doing that, they're firing upon something that they shouldn't, or allowing themselves to be shot at when you've told them not to fire. (There seems like there should be an option for "fire only if attacked", but it's missing). Sometimes they just don't think to run to cover. Having to micro manage your subordinates to avoid them killing themselves becomes an exercise in frustration. Herding cats seems a simpler task.
Overall though, it's a game with endless playability. If you can ignore the silliness of AI, you'll really enjoy it.... especially in multiplayer where at least you'll have actual humans to fight against.

There are a lot of problems for this game, even though it is early access.
Load time: Overall the load time is not that bad, but the thing is there is a Queue that you must wait in for sometimes long periods of time, which I am talking about 10 to 20 minutes of waiting.
Gameplay: This is the main thing I dont like about this game. I thought it would be a pretty amazing pvp game, but what I got was a buggy game not worth the money. Off the bat it is unfair, as you start by parachuting down into the world below looking for a vehicle and supplies. Once you got a gun you'd think it would be pretty easy to aim and shoot, but in this game I find it more difficult than any other game I have played thus far. For a shotgun as an example, you could be standing point  blank firing two shots into your enemy's body and MISS! But by the time you get two shots out, your dead as the physics for guns and vehicles are not great for this game. its basically the same with any other gun, except when your enemies are playing. You must be very dedicated in order to be on a DECENT level with this game, because you can FINALLY get some shots on a person but it wont matter as they will somehow kill you even though they have been damaged more than you, and or someone else will come up behind you and kill you. (Mind you this is mostly on solo)
Vehicles: This one is not so imporant but a big role in the play. Everyone who has played at least an hour knows you need a vehicle most of the time to survive, depending on your spawn. The big issue is that if the glass is broken, IT IS UNUSABLE! The second problem would be that you could be going top speed with your parachute and someone beats you to the vehicle at the last second. It would be a bit easier if you didnt get paralyzed and jump when you land, but eh. If you managed to get a vehicle though, your in for a treat as if you run over a pebble, it is flipping over. No joke you can go over the simplest of terrain and still flip your vehicle.
Conclusion: The game is still in its Early Access and would probably (hope!!!!) fix all these issues in the future, but for now I suggest you wait unless you want to experience how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T this game is at this stage in development.

More power to you if that's what you like to do, but  I for one enjoy Halo, Gears of War, Rainbow Six, and Ghost Recon. So I didn't get that close ranged tactical cover to cover neck snapping stealth urge I needed satisfied. I play Warframe way too much so I wanted something a bit slower and more tactical.  This game seems to be nothing but that.  Too much so for me.  Just download and try it. The first 40 minutes should give you enough to decide rather or not its for you.

Oh damn where to even start. This game is very unique compared to the thousands of FPS games out there. First time players to TF2 will have a good experience overall with the uniquely styled theme and variety of classes to choose from when you first start. Each class has their own strengths and weaknesses that give players an incentive of which class they should play or to suit their playstyle.
The community itself is questionable, but the overall fun and sometimes hilarious experience in game; more than makes up for this. There are a variety of gamemodes to choose from. A trait shared with many FPS games out there. What makes this game standout, compared to others, is that each gamemode itself offers an entirely new experience that regular FPS players will experience like nothing before.  From payload to control points, to even MVM. A tower defense like playstyle in which your team which is composed of you along with 5 other players, must defend a bomb from hundreds upon hundreds of an army of robots.
Another type of experience this game offers, is through the trading system. Where you can trade with the TF2 community for various cosmetics which you can wear for different classes, and unique weapons which can be used in game to offer a different playstyle with a specific class than before. This alone, is another trait that brings in new players who are looking to make some possible real life cash from in game.
Although i don't recommend to play this game for the sole purpose of trading, you will have a better experience by just playing the game itself and choosing which class you prefer to play at the time.
Overall, beyond the fusteration and the sometimes annoying amount of players out there, the fun and amazing gameplay experience is what makes me continue to play this game, along with the amount of cosmetics and tradeable items to work for.
For that, i would give this game a good 7/10 verdict.

Oh damn where to even start. This game is very unique compared to the thousands of FPS games out there. First time players to TF2 will have a good experience overall with the uniquely styled theme and variety of classes to choose from when you first start. Each class has their own strengths and weaknesses that give players an incentive of which class they should play or to suit their playstyle.
The community itself is questionable, but the overall fun and sometimes hilarious experience in game; more than makes up for this. There are a variety of gamemodes to choose from. A trait shared with many FPS games out there. What makes this game standout, compared to others, is that each gamemode itself offers an entirely new experience that regular FPS players will experience like nothing before.  From payload to control points, to even MVM. A tower defense like playstyle in which your team which is composed of you along with 5 other players, must defend a bomb from hundreds upon hundreds of an army of robots.
Another type of experience this game offers, is through the trading system. Where you can trade with the TF2 community for various cosmetics which you can wear for different classes, and unique weapons which can be used in game to offer a different playstyle with a specific class than before. This alone, is another trait that brings in new players who are looking to make some possible real life cash from in game.
Although i don't recommend to play this game for the sole purpose of trading, you will have a better experience by just playing the game itself and choosing which class you prefer to play at the time.
Overall, beyond the fusteration and the sometimes annoying amount of players out there, the fun and amazing gameplay experience is what makes me continue to play this game, along with the amount of cosmetics and tradeable items to work for.
For that, i would give this game a good 7/10 verdict.

I had posted an earlier review which some of you may have read, but deleted it in favor of this one. The game has a lot of potential but has already been ruined by hackers. Like many other online pvp games the system is not secure enough to stop people from piggybacking cheat programs that allow them to dominate the game. I suspected as much after a while and confirmed it by doing an online web search which turned up at least 4 cheat websites. The worst programs are esp which shows the cheater exactly where you are and blows your cover while preserving theirs. You cannot hide from people using this. The second really devastating hack is aimbot. If you play fair you will testify that it is really hard to hit someone from a distance, especially when they are moving. Aimbot eliminates this problem and essentially allows you to hit a target every time no matter how far away. There are others, most notably speed hack and walking through walls. Policing and detection have been ineffective and badly underdone. I estimate 1/5 people are using one or both of these hacks. The end of games is hopeless due to this problem since by then nearly everyone left is a hacker/cheater. Cheating during events is even worse from what I have seen and you would think these would be policed for hacking the most heavily since there is something to gain.
Playing with friends may have some promise left, but eventually you run into the same problem where your honest group gets blown away by cheaters using aimbots. The game mechanics have promise but no matter what the devs achieve, if they can't control the cheating the game will be drowned by this behavior. Honest players who don't want to buy hacks will be driven out and you will be left with a small number of cheaters playing on a level playing field, playing an entirely different kind of game than what was intended with their hacks turned on.
The websites that sell these hacks should be made illegal and the buyers prosecuted or at least fined. It is far to easy to find them on a simple search. They ruin games like these (driving away the honest customers which are the vast majority) which is why they are not popular in general. There needs to be a revolution in gaming that allows the source code not to be tampered with or at least instanly spot this kind of tampering. Until then, games like these will never be playable by honest and principled people.

I would not say that H1Z1: King of the Kill is easily picked up and played. It possesses a steep learning curve and caters greatly to experienced players. With a confusing menu and pregame lobby, many new players would be overwhelmed with not knowing what to do. With no real instruction or direction on how to play the game, newbies end up landing their parachute in a field and running for 5-10 minutes before finding a house that has already been looted of all weapons and supplies. The game also does not instruct the player on how to do basic essentials – like opening up inventory, how to craft, how to view the map, where the compass is, how to heal, where to find gear and weapons, etc. All of these variables add up to a learning curve that chews up and spits out bloodied and mangled new players. However, once all of these things are learned, 8 hours later, the competition is incredibly fun and rewarding to play. No round is the same, and with a huge map to roam, strategies change often.

Oh damn where to even start. This game is very unique compared to the thousands of FPS games out there. First time players to TF2 will have a good experience overall with the uniquely styled theme and variety of classes to choose from when you first start. Each class has their own strengths and weaknesses that give players an incentive of which class they should play or to suit their playstyle.
The community itself is questionable, but the overall fun and sometimes hilarious experience in game; more than makes up for this. There are a variety of gamemodes to choose from. A trait shared with many FPS games out there. What makes this game standout, compared to others, is that each gamemode itself offers an entirely new experience that regular FPS players will experience like nothing before.  From payload to control points, to even MVM. A tower defense like playstyle in which your team which is composed of you along with 5 other players, must defend a bomb from hundreds upon hundreds of an army of robots.
Another type of experience this game offers, is through the trading system. Where you can trade with the TF2 community for various cosmetics which you can wear for different classes, and unique weapons which can be used in game to offer a different playstyle with a specific class than before. This alone, is another trait that brings in new players who are looking to make some possible real life cash from in game.
Although i don't recommend to play this game for the sole purpose of trading, you will have a better experience by just playing the game itself and choosing which class you prefer to play at the time.
Overall, beyond the fusteration and the sometimes annoying amount of players out there, the fun and amazing gameplay experience is what makes me continue to play this game, along with the amount of cosmetics and tradeable items to work for.
For that, i would give this game a good 7/10 verdict.

This game had a whole lot of potential based on the early screenshots, but then Bohemia squandered it when they completely changed everything about it. You can find screenshots jam packed with weapons, attachments, camos, characters, and factions that just do not exist in the game solely because Bohemia wanted to go another course halfway through development.
That might have been an accpetable option, except Bohemia didn't fully commit. Because of this, a lot of the game is just copy-pasted nonsesne. Almost all vehicles use the same HMGs, GMGs, and auto-cannons with the only difference being the hull of the vehicle. All static weapons such as the mortar, GPMG, and anti-tank/anti-air missile launcher are the same in different camos for the different factions. There's maybe a total of 15 unique weapons in the game, all of which are divided into classes and inside these classes there is no variety. An example of this is the MX and Katiba. These each have their respective variants in the CQB, regular, grenadier, and DMR roles, but each one of them is the exact same. They have the same ballistics, same damage, same recoil, same magazine capacity (even though the MX has a much longer, thicker mag than the Katiba,) and hell, even the same round!
Take a look back at ArmA II, you'll notice that each faction has their own ups and downs as far as weapons and vehicles go, but in ArmA III everything feels the exact same and in MANY cases it IS the exact same. They couldn't add a different auto-cannon for each faction, but they sure could add six different fedoras and civilian outfits for you to wear!
Another moronic decision on the part of the devs was to place the game in the future WITHOUT actually adding any futuristic content. Any and all futuristic content was scrapped early on in the development process and then they started adding things that "look futuristic." The Merkava replaces the M1A2 Abrams tank in the least sensible move since Jimmy Carter running for a second term, the Bradley is replaced by the Namer, another Israeli tank, and come to think of it, this entire game is a showcase for Israel. This doesn't make any sense at all in the current iteration of the game where it's spread out amongst all factions, but it made a lot of sense in the original story when Israel was annexed by CSAT and CSAT started using Israeli made weapons and vehicles to supplement their Soviet-made equipment from yester-year. This is a great example why they should've committed to the original story rather than stray away from the original path and create this jumbled mess of a game.
When you get down to the core of it all, all that matters is the gameplay. Unfortunately, that is horrendous, too. The game feels like they watched Rambo on repeat for six weeks straight because instead of combat being fast paced and short lived like it was in in ArmA II, combat is now based on who is a bigger bullet sponge. Players can routinely take six or seven shots before dying, even two shots to the head sometimes does not kill! Full auto is now glorified and not using it is almost a sin because if you don't you're going to be the one in a body-bag. Seriously, they took a simulator game and turned it into Call of Duty.
The encumberance system is another horrible mess. Seriously, your character is not fit for military shape because he can't sprint for more than 20 seconds in full combat load without needing a five minute break, and good luck hitting anything once the enemy has fired a shot in the opposite direction, because your guy is apparently in his first firefight and is already reaching for his entrenching tool to dig all the way to China and is shaking harder than Michael J. Fox with a cold.
Another noticable feature of this game is how poorly optimized it is. Seriously, even with a good gaming rig your online experience will be riddled with framerate drops and, at times, outright freeze-framing.
All in all, I would not recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the ArmA series, because what you will find is far and away from the usual experience.

H1Z1 is a good game, as long as you can get past the seemingly never-ending technical issues involved with playing the game. If you can, you'll soon be thrown into a hunger game-esque arena with toxic gas quickly drawing nearer.
This will test your skills at being able to read a simple map and stay away from gas. Not very challenging at first, but soon becomes so as you're one of many people trapped in the center of the map unable to move due to being surrounded by toxic gas.
The game soon gets your heart beating as you hear people draw near and try to dodge the hail of bullets sprayed in your general direction by getting in your car and pressing your "w" key as fast as possible.
The pace of the game is almost perfect, and the game would be too if it wasn't for technical issues. Overall, however, a good buy and worth the money. Especially if you want to experience the Hunger Games in real life.

The game itself is very well made and is an excellent realistic shooter. Although I haven't seen a bullet drop yet. Headshots in this game are just instant death, and dead is dead, which is a good thing. Bullets also penatrate certain objects (walls/ panels and stuff). Graphics are also very good and map is gigantic huge with incredible details, many cities, peoples and stories. Very nice.
The multiplayer is very much alive currently and is worth playing (jan 2015, at least 100+ games with 40+ players a map). You unlock weapons and stuff based on the level you are. You can buy the unlocked stuff with 'money' which is earned by being inside/ near target, or killing dudes. You maintain your experience, gear and money even if you log out. There are many different types of vehicles to play and scatter throughout the game you can find others to drive as well (also in the campaign).
That said, it is too difficult for myself. There are trillion hotkeys and I haven't been able to command other units. Mostly because they too have zillions different options to use (combat stances, support abilities, and more stuff). I can imagine when you do this in real you just can instantly shout to certain individuals, but here you have to find to right button to open the option list for the action you want him to do, which is somewhere hidden between many other options. I also play games like Battlefield 4 and other fp-shooters, but this one is too frustrating (dying several times a mission) and too difficult (unable to find the target, getting fired upon for no obvious reason) for me.

The reason why I do not recommend this game is simple. A game is not worth playing if you are relieved not to experience a glitch or bug after playing one round of multiplayer.
That is what H1Z1 is, one glitch after another. Dont get me wrong, I have enjoyed playing the game since buying it and believe that the concept is amazing but the fact is that after experiencing a glitch in 2 of every 3 matches (that forces me to stop playing) has caused me to write this negative review.
The amount of times that I have experienced the "car bug" (what I am now calling it) is unbelievable and plain pathetic. What this bug does is extreemly frustrating as it kicks you out of the car but locks you in the position that you were kicked out, preventing you from moving and forcing you to quit the game. Its sad because now I'm actually scared to get into a car as I have a fear of getting this bug again (which has happened to me in 2 out of 3 games that I play).
The game is an amazing concept, the combat requires skill and the game can give you an amazing time to be had with friends (all the things i like in a game) but in the end the game just frustrates me and causes me to have a miserable time, this is why I cannot recommend the game.

After putting in over 800 hours into this game's predecessor, Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate, this game plays with the gameplay mechanics a bit while still retaining the good feel of victory after each hunt.
Like the other games in the series, the main gameplay focuses around your character hunting monsters, with the key focus of avoiding their attacks and attacking at opportune moments between their attacks, often times hitting their weak points for massive damage. And, like every game in the series, you can't heal and attack super quickly; you need to get out of the way of an incoming attack and heal, then continue avoiding attacks until the opportune moment to strike.
There's a smaller weapon variety in this game, but each weapon is still unique in how it plays, as how you attack with each weapon slightly differs, so I'm glad they retained that feature. Another feature that's also in this game is the limited inventory space, so you have to manage your inventory as you progress; you can't hold everything, after all.
One thing I'm sort of iffy about is the limited hunter rank; in the previous game, it was 999, but in this game it's only 20. This makes it much easier to cap your rank, and it doesn't feel as rewarding, but the grind it takes to get there is a lot quicker so I guess that's a plus.
Perhaps the best part of the entire franchise is that the main 'large monsters' get their own battle theme, and this game is no exception, providing intense battle music for the two flagship boss monsters, as well as the usual recurring map theme for regular hunts.
One mechanic that I abused greatly seemed to have been removed until the final boss, and that is the popular tactic known as sleep bombing; towards endgame, you're given the only weapon with the sleeping status effect. Nothing quite satisfies like putting the monster to sleep then destroying it with one devastating unseen strike to finish it off.
All in all, this game plays quite differently than the other Monster Hunter games, but still retains many of its core features and that's why I recommend it. It has significantly less content than the other Monster Hunter games, but it's also significantly cheaper so it balances out nicely.

Not too sure what to write here so here's a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings. :)

After putting in over 800 hours into this game's predecessor, Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate, this game plays with the gameplay mechanics a bit while still retaining the good feel of victory after each hunt.
Like the other games in the series, the main gameplay focuses around your character hunting monsters, with the key focus of avoiding their attacks and attacking at opportune moments between their attacks, often times hitting their weak points for massive damage. And, like every game in the series, you can't heal and attack super quickly; you need to get out of the way of an incoming attack and heal, then continue avoiding attacks until the opportune moment to strike.
There's a smaller weapon variety in this game, but each weapon is still unique in how it plays, as how you attack with each weapon slightly differs, so I'm glad they retained that feature. Another feature that's also in this game is the limited inventory space, so you have to manage your inventory as you progress; you can't hold everything, after all.
One thing I'm sort of iffy about is the limited hunter rank; in the previous game, it was 999, but in this game it's only 20. This makes it much easier to cap your rank, and it doesn't feel as rewarding, but the grind it takes to get there is a lot quicker so I guess that's a plus.
Perhaps the best part of the entire franchise is that the main 'large monsters' get their own battle theme, and this game is no exception, providing intense battle music for the two flagship boss monsters, as well as the usual recurring map theme for regular hunts.
One mechanic that I abused greatly seemed to have been removed until the final boss, and that is the popular tactic known as sleep bombing; towards endgame, you're given the only weapon with the sleeping status effect. Nothing quite satisfies like putting the monster to sleep then destroying it with one devastating unseen strike to finish it off.
All in all, this game plays quite differently than the other Monster Hunter games, but still retains many of its core features and that's why I recommend it. It has significantly less content than the other Monster Hunter games, but it's also significantly cheaper so it balances out nicely.

Not too sure what to write here so here's a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings. :)

This is quite possibly the most emotional shooter I've ever played, and it's not because of the campaign.
Crowd around, children, it's story time.
One day, not so long ago, my squad had just destroyed an anti-air battery. Our pilot landed, and the rest of the squad boarded one by one. I was about to get in when the rockets started flying.
The chopper lifted off, with my pilot saying that he would return in a few minutes. Unwilling to die before then, I rushed to the nearest cover, a small house by a narrow road. I entered to find a ten year-old player who had also been left behind. He explained that he was a sniper and invited me to join his "clan".
I politely declined, explaining that my own squad was inbound. As I finished, a Ghost Hawk flew over the horizon. My squad had arrived.
This noble child soldier and I were sprinting to the helicopter when the bullets started hitting. The sniper screamed as a 6.5 mm cartridge entered his leg. His shrieks for help were cut short by one final burst of carbine fire as I climbed in the transport.
My new friend was dead.
10/10, would experience survivor guilt again.

Don't mistake this game for an FPS, some people enter into this game expecting COD ...it's not. ARMA is a full battlefield simulator which it does well at. In ARMA you're not meant to feel invincible, if you don't take cover you'll die, if you don't communicate with your squad you'll die. It has an insane learning curve that will take most people a long time to get used to, but only makes it very satisfying once you finally figure out how to fly or use artillery or...anything. The complicated controls at first can seem annoying but once you're used to them you'll be grateful you can stick your head up just enough to see an enemy out of a window without exposing your whole body.
The games mod-ability makes it possible to play an infinite array of game modes making it difficult to get truly boring. While there is a battlefield like mod called king of the hill the size of the maps alone makes the game vastly more complex and that's saying nothing of the array of vehicles that can completely alter the game from just one player knowing how to fly or range a sniper rifle.
Unfortunately the ARMA engine is well known for how glitchy it can get, Most of this has been ironed out and the presence of hackers ruining servers has been greatly reduced since early access. At times clipping through a wall or falling through the floor of a building still happens but it's not so common that it ruins things.
At the end of the day the game requires being patient and on your toes while communicating what you see with teammates. The different mods and game modes give the game infinite potential but the glitches can create issues sometimes. ARMA 3 is a military sim not "insert FPS here" don't get attached to scores and if you find yourself complaining over global that someone using a plane is "cheap" or a "noob"  close the game and reevaluate who you want to be in life.

Oh ArmA. ArmA, ArmA, ArmA. The abusive relationship we have shared over the past 4 games has become more abusive, and less fun, and all it took was one title. One title full of empty promises, and most likely just a tech demo to fix the engine up for DayZ 2. Let me elaborate on my disdain for what used to be one of my favorite game series, and the company that I used to respect above every other.
The quick and dirty, would I recommend ArmA 3? Not by a mile. Sub-30 price tag, sure, you'll get your monies worth. But even for all the modders trying to save it, this is not a complete game. You should not have to pay 60 dollars to go and download a number of COMMUNITY created additions to feel like you actually have a full fledged product. If some of that money went to those modders, then I'd say support THEM, not BI. But it doesn't. Imagine buying a car, but having to go out and purchase the doors and steering wheel separately. Sure the car runs, but just how useable is it?
A quick glance at my steam page would reveal that I highly praised BI's adventurous approach to ArmA 2, and OA. I loved ArmA with a blazing passion, even though it's considered the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of the series. OFP shared a warm place in my heart as the birth of one of my favorite mil-sims. Sure, since OFP, the series has had its caveats and nuances, but you quickly learned to take them with the massive amount of fun the games provided. So where did ArmA 3 go wrong? What could one title do to tear my respect for 3 other games (+ 2 Expansions & DLC)? Well, lets start with the company and work our way up. You see, riding on the heels of the massive success that DayZ was thanks to word of mouth and LPs, BI somewhere seems to have got it in their head that the same business practices most AAA companies do (Incomplete Games for Full Price, DLC strategies), could be done to their small communities. And you know what? They were right. We all bought into it. BI slowly came to realize that they could do less work, and still make more money, because their communities could turn nowhere else. What amazes me most about DayZ, besides the fact that it is still in Alpha after almost 2 years, and that it's lead creator left, is that all it really did was show what ArmA 2 was already capable of. Massive, persistent worlds with Mil-Sim themes. Just, with zombies.
But, this is not a review of DayZ, this a review of ArmA 3. Any ArmA community member worth his or her grain of salt will remember all the broken promises that now lay at ArmA 3's feet. Disguising as the enemy? Gone. The Railgun tank, one of the coolest features at E3, and the only one making the future worth giving a damn about? Poof. All the underwater showcases, hinting at perhaps real naval gameplay? Nope. Planes? We got 3. Funny thing is, all you Deluxe Edition owners should open up that Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures manual it comes with sometime, and view all the planes we should have had. The reskinned C-130 and F-35? Fugetta about it. That's right, we couldn't even get recycled content.
Now, let me be fair, ArmA 3's engine is a massive improvement over previous series entries. And OFP/ArmA has always been one of those games where the community really takes it the final step with endless content. But Vanilla, the games were usually very playable, and very enjoyable. This is where ArmA 3 comes up the shortest. While the engine is great, and getting better with each patch, not only are we still denied even a basic amount of content, but the underlying issues since OFP are still there. 2013/2014, we still have an action menu. BI, please. Not to mention that AI has somehow found a way to get worse with all these improvements, rather than better.
You know, some people actually say ArmA 2 people were spoiled because we had OFP and ArmA 1's content all rolled into one. I find it hard to give sympathy to the people whose job it is to create content and games. Who get paid for it. In closing I will say this. ArmA 3, as a game, is complete and total BS. ArmA 3, as a platform, for people to show their skills in modeling, texturing, and coding, fantastic. If you want ArmA 3, do it to support people who make great content. Just don't expect a full fledged game, for the full fledged price.

So I've finally reach 1000 hours in this game. Much of it is from the Tough break update onward, though i did play before. But; Here is my review of the game in it's current state; as of 6/14/17.
Team Fortress 2 is a free-to-play, class-based shoot-em-up. I won't go into detail, but with 9 classes to choose from there is quite the variety. And, with the 126 unique weapons, there's even more variety with different loadouts and combinations, making a load of fun and interesting playstyles!
When i first really got into it during the Tough Break update, it was and still is one of my favorite updates. Now i won't say it was perfect, but it felt, to me, much more stable then than it currently is. Kills and deaths didn't seem cheap or unearned, (Unless it's from a random crit...) and with the contracts, it always felt like satisfying to get, say, 3 clean headshots, and hear that ticking of the Points bar just raising, and eventually dinging. It was always a strive and a struggle to gain those points and reach the top, and even fill out the bonus bar for the chance at a better reward! Now said reward may not have been great, always, but to me that didn't matter as much, it was just so much fun to me to get those done, and I felt accomplished. That's what got me into the game, and made it so close to my heart. And it lasted quite a long time; From December 17, 2015, to April 11th of the following year.
Just months later, Meet your Match was released. And, while, it didn't do so well and eventually became more balanced and more enjoyable, sadly it did change many things that personally i didn't agree with, though there were things I
enjoy, as well. Even now, after the Halloween and Christmas updates, which were wuite small, many things now feel unfair, and aren't that fun. Now i hate to be That Guy, who craps on Casual and Matchmaking, but there are many many flaws with it still.
The queue times have been fixed and decreased, which is good. But, once in a game, many times I find that few people are in it, and the game starts with about 6 or 7 players on each team. Sometimes less. And very rarely do I see new players joining into the matches once it's started, so games tend to be fairly boring for me. Or, you can get games which are filled with 11 or 12 players on each team, as it should be. However, most times the games are highly unbalanced, and one team or the other simply gets steam rolled, and it's un fun, for either party, even. I still often see script kiddies and hackers on the servers, as well. Though they aren't as often as they used to, or as difficult to get rid of, they are still an issue. (Though Valve has shown they do care about this issue, there have been multiple VAC-ban waves in recent months) Despite these issues, i can still find myself hopping on, playing a match or two, and having fun.
As for the gameplay itself, minus Matchmaking, there are also quite a few things i do not enjoy. Going back to my statement earlier on the many, varied styles of gameplay, some are simply un-fun to play against. Now i know there are some people that will simply say 'Git gud' or referr to the fact I am a Medic Main, these things are issues i genuinely believe should be altered. Things such as 'W+M1' Pyros, or Demoknights. Hell, even Beggar's Bazooka Soldiers aren't that fun sometimes. Random crits, of course, is nearly everyone's pet-peeve, as they are ju8st that, random, and don't really require that much skill, or any requirement at all, really. Hitboxes and registration are also things Valve should look into, sometimes it feels i could have not possibly been killed, such as being backstabbed by a spy that is clearly in front of me, or being killed by someone when you're around a corner or behind a wall.
Once again, despite many of these issues and problems, I can always find fun in the game. And, with a brand new update just around the corner, which is promising to be one of the largest, I have very high hopes for what the TFTeam has in store for us! And, i know I listed off almost only issues with the game, but I simply cannot list off everything I DO enjoy about the game! With how much time i've poured into it, (Though it's not as much as others would have in 3 years or so) I've enjoyed just about every update and every weapon at one point, and every class and play style!
Anyways, I highly reccomend this game, especially for a free to play game!

I posted my original review back before the Eden editor was released, and I feel like I should touch on that. Mission editing has come so far since I initially bought the game, the sheer amount of options is outstanding. I'm able to fine-tune placement of enemies and set up environments with a finesse I never had back with the old 2D editor. The streamlined interface makes it so much easier to tweak settings like journal entries and listed objectives. However, I find the tutorials next to useless, luckily I'm an ArmA veteran of several years and am already largely familiar with Bohemia's scripting commands and interface, so it's not much of a problem to me (though I imagine it will hinder aspiring mission creators, for those of you new to ArmA and want to dive into Eden, go online and look up one of the many community-made guides, they're outstanding).
Let me say, however, that I do NOT appreciate the new, at lack of a better term, "on-disk" (in-program?) DLC. I hate that all the content for Apex and the other DLC's are in my game, on my hard disk, but "locked". I can't use the map that is taking up space on my hard drive, and all of the vehicles are present but undrivable to me. The guns and units are usable but an annoying overlay pops up during missions that can distract you and even get you killed (thanks Bohemia, I really wanted to die after 30 minutes of careful planning and execution thanks to a pop-up ad IN THE GAME I ALREADY BOUGHT). I don't care about the DLC, if I want it I'll buy it, but don't you think for a second that it's at all okay to stick it in the game and then charge me to use the files that are already present on my computer. I want Apex, but I almost don't want ot buy it out of spite.
I hardly play Multiplayer, in any game, dunno why I just don't....ARMA 3 is one of the three games I player multiplayer in. Here's a story of that....
Just...insane. The realism of ARMA 3 coupled with the fact that I was fighting alongside guys halfway across the world who were just as invested into the mission as I was made our plight that much more intense.
As a veteran of the ARMA series I can attest to the progress Bohemia has made in ARMA 3. Almost (ALMOST) everything I griped about in previous games were fixed...including some that actually made me stop playing for a while. I was a little♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at the lack of units at first, but then I remembered the crap-ton of user-made addons avalible in the Workshop and on Armaholic. I now have units from the cold war up to the Vanilla units of the future. I can play any war that I want and I can't think of any other game that can do that.
The island of Altis is HUGE, Stratis is pretty big but meh...it's a fruit fly compared to the Budgie of Altis (look up the difference, it's a suitable comparison...don't you judge me). There's a lot of space to destroy, with a variety of different areas allowing for different combat. You can do anything from marching across a shallow river to an intense firefight in a city.
The variety of fighting is outstanding. Being able to fight as a soldier, then go to a tank commander, then a gunship pilot, and a plane pilot, then to a special operator....it's outstanding. I've played in user-made campaigns where you literally cover every aspect of the war. To sum it up, it's like starring in a dozen war movies on your own.
If you've got patience and a desire to learn you can take a spin at the mission editor. It has a STEEEEEP learning curve, it'll require some serious investment to get good at. I'm still learning the new Eden editor but overall it's a lot easier to use than the previous editor, but it's still difficult to learn for newbies. The editor allows for almost unlimited replayability, once you're done with the vanilla campaign and whatever custom ones you downloaded, you can simply hop into the editor and make your own!
Now time for the gripes
There's some aspects of the game that are...difficult to cusp, mostly in the editor. I feel like the game is actually all that finished yet, I won't go into detail about this but there's features that don't seem all quite there yet. I also don't appreciate minor DLC's being thrown out there with only a bit of content. I liked it better when Bohemia released a DLC with an entire new army and several new maps, like Operation Arrowhead (which was actually stand-alone), British Armed Forces, PMC, and Army of the Czech Republic. I haven't sunk any money into them because I'm holding out for "ARMA 3 Pan-Asian War" or "ARMA 3 World War III"...or, something of that strain....something with new armies, maps, and weapons instead of just a few new features. (To specify, I'm not saying that the DLC's are bad but I'm not willing to pay for them until something monumental comes out).
All in all this is an outstanding game without peer (say all you want about CoD and Battlefield, I love both franchises and have sunk many hours into their various incarnations, but they don't hold a candle to the glory of Armed Assault). If you're a serious gamer, this is your game. Military fan? This is your game. Modding fan? This is your game. Micro-transactions to restock energy and make moves? SCREW OFF AND GO BACK TO YOUR PHONE. You're not welcome here and we'd prefer if you kept your micro-transaction covered fingers out of our bowl of Steam.

Wow. What can I say about ArmA 3. (Armed Assault 3, that is) This is an absolute phenominon of a game, and that goes beyond the core gameplay and fun factor delivered in the executable file itself, but in the knowledge gained from partaking on this veritable adventure. First, there is the transferablle tactical expertise, which when gathered from playtime in this game can be moved to other games like CSGO, or PUBG, or even the Witcher 3, to further enhance your experience there. Upon seeing the loading screen of this game, your mind is injected with subtle yet core changes to its strategic stratephos, allowing calculations on a grand scale to be conducted in lightning speed. Next, we see that the game actually makes you an immediate comedian. Simply saying in game catchphrases like, "Contact Contact Contact", "Im taking overwatch", or "Calling in CAS" will have your friends, family, significant others, and neighbors sprawled on the ground laughing. Finally, this game gives you a complete rudimentary understanding of everything military based, think of it as being in the army for a year or two. When you see a veteran in public, you can now approach with a wide variety of conversational topics, such as PTSD, or how black NPCs are worse than white ones. You can tell them you fully understand how heavy a pack of gear weighs, and how long average in operation transport flights take. If you dont understand some of the "terminology" ive been interspersing throughout this review, I think that just goes to show how simple minded your brain can be pre-ArmA 3 experience. (Armed Assault 3, that is) Talk to me when you barrel roll your first helicopter inside of a friendly APC while blasting trap music over the stereo system while 600 invisible objects explode around you, sending you flying under the map, while your CO applauds you on your incredible dedication to immersion and realism. Silly casual. Maybe (Scoffs) COD, or (Chuckles) Battlefield is more your thing.

Team Fortress 2 is an interesting game that has lead many into thousands of hours of gameplay and entertainment. Although the game fails providing a somewhat-decent tutorial, it is easy to pick up and hard to master. This makes the game fun to progress into skill levels. With 150 levels in Casual you spend hours upon hours in games attempting to rank up and when you're done, there is competetive. Frankly, this is not something to go to looking for serious gameplay. Currently, it saw as a joke and even new players tend to click the big button. If neither casual nor competetive suits you, there is numerous community servers that have different custom gamemodes like surfing, and deathmatch. Another option is MvM, or Mann vs. Machine, which consists of a team verses bots, untimately getting harder as the match progresses. To win items on completetion of tours, you must pay 1 dollar to enter. There is also an option where you recieve no items but enter the gamemode. With all these options combined, I have invested a thousand hours on end, never suffering from boredom. I would highly recommend this game for a try. It is free, what's the harm?

Wow. What can I say about ArmA 3. (Armed Assault 3, that is) This is an absolute phenominon of a game, and that goes beyond the core gameplay and fun factor delivered in the executable file itself, but in the knowledge gained from partaking on this veritable adventure. First, there is the transferablle tactical expertise, which when gathered from playtime in this game can be moved to other games like CSGO, or PUBG, or even the Witcher 3, to further enhance your experience there. Upon seeing the loading screen of this game, your mind is injected with subtle yet core changes to its strategic stratephos, allowing calculations on a grand scale to be conducted in lightning speed. Next, we see that the game actually makes you an immediate comedian. Simply saying in game catchphrases like, "Contact Contact Contact", "Im taking overwatch", or "Calling in CAS" will have your friends, family, significant others, and neighbors sprawled on the ground laughing. Finally, this game gives you a complete rudimentary understanding of everything military based, think of it as being in the army for a year or two. When you see a veteran in public, you can now approach with a wide variety of conversational topics, such as PTSD, or how black NPCs are worse than white ones. You can tell them you fully understand how heavy a pack of gear weighs, and how long average in operation transport flights take. If you dont understand some of the "terminology" ive been interspersing throughout this review, I think that just goes to show how simple minded your brain can be pre-ArmA 3 experience. (Armed Assault 3, that is) Talk to me when you barrel roll your first helicopter inside of a friendly APC while blasting trap music over the stereo system while 600 invisible objects explode around you, sending you flying under the map, while your CO applauds you on your incredible dedication to immersion and realism. Silly casual. Maybe (Scoffs) COD, or (Chuckles) Battlefield is more your thing.

Arma 3 is a ridiculously complicated military simulator which includes 7 buttons just to look around (that is if you're too special to use the mouse like everyone else). You can play through a bunch of single player scenarios which subject you to taking down the odd bad guy, while knowing that a single stray bullet could end your life. These scenarios are all pretty much the same, move on to the next town, take out the five random guys that are wandering around armed with assault rifles, then repeat. It's multiplayer that makes this game shine, a bunch of modded servers like the immensely popular 'Altis Life' mode in which you can play as a civilian or cop. As a civilian you'll buy your drivers license, set off to a life of adventure, get robbed, stripped naked and kneecapped before being abandonded in the desert. In your next life you'll probably head over to the cocaine field to try and make some easy drug money, right? Wrong. As you fill your pockets with unprocessed cocaine (which look suspiciously like rotten cabbages) you'll likely run into a group of like-minded rebels who will make it their business to brutally kill you and take all of your items which you worked so hard for. Then you respawn with nothing and do it all again. As a cop you'll try to stop this from happening, but you'll probably just taze the wrong guy, run him over, then try to pretend like you never did it. You'll brutally murder a bunch of people completely on accident, that is to say, you pull a guy over for speeding, he annoys you so much that you shoot him with your tazer. Then he has a bad reaction to the tazer and the next thing you know you're cleaning up a dead body.
Honestly, do I need to say anymore?

Arma series has always had faithful fanbase and for a good reason, while not the most optimized or most fluid gameplay wise, they've brought a one-of-a-kind twist to whole FPS genre with realism and simulation.
Arma 3 continues this trend and does so very well.
This game offers INSANE value in terms of varied gamemodes. There is an endless ocean of great and not so great mods for arma which alter the gameplay in many different ways. Mods are the reason why you should buy this game, you quite literally get dozens of games' worth of content by buying Arma 3. You can play survival, role play, play massive war scenarios, just shoot for fun, it's all there.
Visually this is one of the most impressive looking games to date. Huge maps with absolutely massive draw distance, fair amount of texture detail and good lighting effects really add up to a spectacular feel. Night time is especially impressive with really dark nights and tracer shots lighting up the sky. All this comes with a hefty price though, this game really brings even most poverful computers down to their knees. Optimization isn't great this time around either and multiplayer performance suffers quite a blow. Please do your research before buying so you at least have some clue if this'll run at all.
Sound assets are good, guns sound beefy and other little details such as bullet impacts really bring immersion and feel of danger to gunfights. Built in VOIP communication is absolutely necessary and it's done well, with VOD and everything. Voice chat does get bit crackly sometimes though.
Gameplay has always been both the high and low point of arma series and this doesn't change. Luckily enough some features are bit better this time and I especially like the new inventory layout. Controls are still somewhat clunky and mousewheel has way more functions bound to it than ever necessary. Also arma doors are legendary for being annyoying... Buildings have some clipping issues which combined with awkward doors and bit jerky movement can lead to sticky situations. Vehicle controls are for the most part fine, but cars blow up if you look at them funny.
Gunplay is a thing I've always loved in Arma. Realistic effective distances for guns and decent bullet physics make shooting and hitting really satisfying. Assault rifles can still be very, very deadly up to 500m or so and draw distance allows for extremely long range sniping (sniping is real hard though, don't expect point and click).  Combine this with good gun sounds and visuals and we've got one impressive package. Close combat is sometimes bit iffy in multiplayer as lag and desyncing can make hit detection not work perfectly and it's common situation for 2 players to end up killing each other in CQB.
This is a war simulation game though, so if you come expecting some fast paced shooting action for a 30 minute session every now and then you should probably look elsewhere. Arma 3 takes dedication, and even if there are some gamemodes designed for casual action, they're still slow paced compared to other shooters. People camp for hours just to snipe you in perfect oppourtunity, people try to avoid fair engagements, you will die to players you never thought were anywhere near you, you will be brought down by massive hail of bullets from attack helicopter mile high in the sky.
If you're fine with the things in last paragraph and have a good PC, get Arma 3, you won't regret it.

It's the dead of night on the CSAT-occupied island of Stratis, and the peaceful darkness is about to explode into chaos. I'm leading one of two spec-ops teams on a mission to liberate the leader of a local guerrilla faction and return him to the much larger island of Altis. A British squad is in charge of the actual rescue. Our job is to cause as much trouble across the island as possible to distract the CSAT forces and give the British the opening they need.
Over the next hour, that's precisely what I do. Inserting by boat from the northwest coast, I head south and raid an ammo dump before cutting across to the eastern shore to destroy a heliport. Then my squad suppresses an enemy encampment from a hillside near the centre of the island as I swoop in from the west to flank them. Yet before we can regroup, my entire team is killed by reinforcements descending from the north, and the British still need more time to complete their mission. Alone, I rush to the southernmost tip of the island, where I blow up a fortified anti-air position before escaping by riding a quad bike back through the swarming enemy forces to the extraction point, where the boat takes me home.
Arguably the biggest complaint about Bohemia Interactive's post-Flashpoint games is that their campaigns haven't used the magnificent landscapes they create to their full potential. The first Arma's campaign was a hastily cobbled-together disappointment, while it took a certain zombie-survival mod to harness the austere and foreboding power of Arma 2's Chernarus. That Arma 3 uses half an island for just one of its twenty-odd missions is indicative of Bohemia's effort to resolve this ongoing issue. Indeed, taken as a whole, Arma 3 strives to make this deep and impenetrable military simulator series a more comprehensive, more engaging and more user-friendly experience. It isn't completely successful, but I had an awful lot of fun watching it try.
There are also a lot of mods that can be added in to make you experience more intense and satisfying, such as various weapons, vehicles and missions. The mods that have got me hooked right now are the Life Mods (such as Altis Life, Takistan Life and Arma 3 Life) and the Wasteland mod. I wish i could talk more about them but i seem to have ran out of room in this here text box, but all in all great game 8/10

It's the dead of night on the CSAT-occupied island of Stratis, and the peaceful darkness is about to explode into chaos. I'm leading one of two spec-ops teams on a mission to liberate the leader of a local guerrilla faction and return him to the much larger island of Altis. A British squad is in charge of the actual rescue. Our job is to cause as much trouble across the island as possible to distract the CSAT forces and give the British the opening they need.
Over the next hour, that's precisely what I do. Inserting by boat from the northwest coast, I head south and raid an ammo dump before cutting across to the eastern shore to destroy a heliport. Then my squad suppresses an enemy encampment from a hillside near the centre of the island as I swoop in from the west to flank them. Yet before we can regroup, my entire team is killed by reinforcements descending from the north, and the British still need more time to complete their mission. Alone, I rush to the southernmost tip of the island, where I blow up a fortified anti-air position before escaping by riding a quad bike back through the swarming enemy forces to the extraction point, where the boat takes me home.
Arguably the biggest complaint about Bohemia Interactive's post-Flashpoint games is that their campaigns haven't used the magnificent landscapes they create to their full potential. The first Arma's campaign was a hastily cobbled-together disappointment, while it took a certain zombie-survival mod to harness the austere and foreboding power of Arma 2's Chernarus. That Arma 3 uses half an island for just one of its twenty-odd missions is indicative of Bohemia's effort to resolve this ongoing issue. Indeed, taken as a whole, Arma 3 strives to make this deep and impenetrable military simulator series a more comprehensive, more engaging and more user-friendly experience. It isn't completely successful, but I had an awful lot of fun watching it try.
There are also a lot of mods that can be added in to make you experience more intense and satisfying, such as various weapons, vehicles and missions. The mods that have got me hooked right now are the Life Mods (such as Altis Life, Takistan Life and Arma 3 Life) and the Wasteland mod. I wish i could talk more about them but i seem to have ran out of room in this here text box, but all in all great game 8/10

Arma 3 teamwork and the AMAZING spotlight
Had a blast last night working together with my squad and never knew how deadly the spotlights on heli's could be...
During the first round of king of the hill, there was only about 30 players total, so I took to my beloved Hellcat chopper to help spot the enemy for my squad. Another teamate flew a Pawnee with rockets and guns and as I found targets hiding in Kavela I would call out thier location and within 15 secs or less our Pawnee would come in and lay waste to the enemy.
We dominated everyone that round. It was daylight so spotting was pretty easy and if the Pawnee couldnt get to them, our ground forces would move into the area to flush them out. The entire team was working together calling out targets waiting for the incoming rocket barrage!!
The next match was even better. Same map but night time with almost no visibility on the ground...this is where it got really fun. I switched on my giant spotlight finding and hovering over targets waiting for the Pawnee to swoop in and take em out. We must have gotten 30+ kills this way.
I felt like the police going after criminals spotlighting enemies as they ran from building to building, cover to cover trying to hide form my spotlight. After a while they figured out they needed to hide from that annoying heli pilot shining a giant light in thier faces.
So many times I would find an enemy on rooftops trying to hide where I would come in and light the whole building up. They were getting soooo mad, would either have to run and hide or would try to shoot my light out so they werent so exposed, which of course never worked out in thier favor. Many times I would follow with my light the enemy from building to building, across the city tracking them until our forces could kill or flush them out.
In 20 years of gaming this has to be one of the best gaming experiences in my life. The pawnee pilot even mentioned he felt bad for killing them after I would spot them. The enemy knew if that light found them they were done for.
Its funny something as simple as a light could be so fun and deadly...10/10 for Amra 3!!!!!!!

A truly astonishing modern masterpiece that's not for the faint hearted. This is not a game for those who like running around spraying bullets COD style. Often you will be fighting at 500m range and a single shot from an unseen enemy willtake you out. This is a game about meticulous planning, strategy and tactics. Played in a large, open world, the graphics are superb leading to a great feeling of immersion. There is no single way to approach any mission, which means you can often spend 50 attempts to get it right. The only downsides to an otherwise flawless game are the occaisonal buggy script, which means reloading a saved game, limited choice of weapons and rather unintelligable UI for loadout / planning. But these flaws are quickly overlooked by the absolute magnificence of the rest of the game.
